In March 2014, the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) ''reported'' a major Ebola outbreak in [[Guinea]], a western African nation,<ref name="CDC2014Out">{{Cite web |date=1 August 2014 |title=Guidelines for Evaluation of US Patients Suspected of Having Ebola Virus Disease |url=http://emergency.cdc.gov/han/han00364.asp |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808075214/http://emergency.cdc.gov/han/han00364.asp |archive-date=8 August 2014 |access-date=5 August 2014 |website=CDC}}</ref> the disease then rapidly spread to the neighboring countries of [[Liberia]] and [[Sierra Leone]] with smaller outbreaks occurring in [[Senegal]], [[Nigeria]], and [[Mali]]; the resulting '''[[West African Ebola virus epidemic]]''' is the largest Ebola outbreak ('''''cases and deaths''''') ever documented.<ref name="CDC2014Out" />

==Background==
{{Ebola virus disease epidemic}}
{{Main|West African Ebola virus epidemic}}
Researchers believe that a 2-year-old boy who lived in the village of [[Meliandou]], [[Guéckédou Prefecture]], [[Guinea]] was the [[index case]] of the then current [[Ebola virus disease]] epidemic. The boy died in December 2013. His mother, sister, and grandmother then became ill with similar symptoms and also died. Although Ebola represents a significant public health problem in sub-Saharan Africa and was documented<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Formenty |first=Pierre |display-authors=etal |date=Feb 1999 |title=Ebola Virus Outbreak among Wild Chimpanzees Living in a Rain Forest of Côte d'Ivoire |journal=J. Infect. Dis. |volume=179 |issue=s1 |pages=S120–S126 |bibcode=1999JInfD.179S.120F |doi=10.1086/514296 |pmid=9988175 |doi-access=free}}</ref> in [[Tai Forest]] [[Common chimpanzee|chimpanzees]], only one case had been reported in humans in [[West Africa]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Le Guenno |first1=B |last2=Formenty |first2=P |last3=Wyers |first3=M |display-authors=etal |date=1995 |title=Isolation and partial characterisation of a new strain of Ebola virus |url=http://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736%2895%2990925-7/abstract |journal=Lancet |volume=345 |issue=8960 |pages=1271–1274 |doi=10.1016/s0140-6736(95)90925-7 |pmid=7746057 |s2cid=38897209 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> With this background and in the context of poor public health systems,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Helen Epstein |date=18 December 2014 |title=Ebola in Liberia: An Epidemic of Rumors |url=http://www.nybooks.com/articles/archives/2014/dec/18/ebola-liberia-epidemic-rumors/ |journal=The New York Review of Books |volume=61 |issue=20 |access-date=6 January 2015}}</ref> the early cases were mis-diagnosed as diseases more common to the area. Thus [[Ebola virus disease]] spread for several months before it was recognized as such.<ref name="Baize-2014">{{Cite journal |last1=Baize |first1=Sylvain |last2=Pannetier |first2=Delphine |last3=Oestereich |first3=Lisa |last4=Rieger |first4=Toni |date=16 April 2014 |title=Emergence of Zaire Ebola Virus Disease in Guinea&nbsp;— Preliminary Report |journal=New England Journal of Medicine |volume=371 |issue=15 |pages=1418–25 |doi=10.1056/NEJMoa1404505 |pmid=24738640 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Tracing Ebola's Breakout to an African 2-Year-Old">{{Cite news |last1=Grady |first1=Denise |last2=Fink |first2=Sheri |date=9 August 2014 |title=Tracing Ebola's Breakout to an African 2-Year-Old |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/08/10/world/africa/tracing-ebolas-breakout-to-an-african-2-year-old.html |access-date=14 August 2014 |work=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> In late October 2014, the boy was later identified as Emile Ouamouno.<ref>{{Cite news |date=28 October 2014 |title=Ebola: Patient zero was a toddler in Guinea - CNN.com |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2014/10/28/health/ebola-patient-zero/index.html |access-date=21 November 2014 |work=CNN}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=28 October 2014 |title=Ebola Patient Zero: Emile Ouamouno Of Guinea First To Contract Disease |url=http://www.ibtimes.com/ebola-patient-zero-emile-ouamouno-guinea-first-contract-disease-1714698 |access-date=21 November 2014 |website=International Business Times}}</ref> In a Tuesday, December 30, 2014 online world news story article by Richard Ingham from the [[Agence France-Presse]] (AFP) that was featured on the [[MSN]] homepage, it was revealed that a tree in the area where children had played at, playing with insect-eating [[free-tailed bat]]s and hunting and grilling them to eat (they are a cousin of another well-known Ebola reservoir, the [[fruit bat]], whose role in this outbreak is not as clear), is believed to be the point where human infection&nbsp;– likely by the bats&nbsp;– with Ebola in this current outbreak occurred, the 'ground zero' of the epidemic. This is not yet known decisively, but scientists have enough knowledge to go public with the story.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hollow tree was Ebola's Ground Zero: scientists |url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/world/hollow-tree-was-ebolas-ground-zero-scientists/ar-BBhlS79 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304060935/http://www.msn.com/en-us/news/world/hollow-tree-was-ebolas-ground-zero-scientists/ar-BBhlS79 |archive-date=2016-03-04 |access-date=2015-09-04 |website=[[MSN]]}}</ref>

==Timeline of reported cases and deaths==
{{See also|Ebola virus epidemic in West Africa timeline}}

===Data sources===
Data comes from reports by the World Health Organization Global Alert and Response Unit<ref group="Resource">{{Cite web |title=Disease Outbreak News (DONs) |url=http://who.int/csr/don/en/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030125005720/http://www.who.int/csr/don/en/ |archive-date=January 25, 2003 |access-date=11 April 2015 |website=Global Alert and Response (GAR) |publisher=[[WHO]]}}{{Fastdelta}}</ref> and the WHO's Regional Office for Africa.<ref name="autogenerated2" group="Resource">{{Cite web |title=Disease Outbreak News |url=http://www.afro.who.int/en/clusters-a-programmes/dpc/epidemic-a-pandemic-alert-and-response/outbreak-news.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150424072105/http://www.afro.who.int/en/clusters-a-programmes/dpc/epidemic-a-pandemic-alert-and-response/outbreak-news.html |archive-date=24 April 2015 |access-date=11 April 2015 |website=Regional Office for Africa |publisher=[[WHO]]}}{{Fastdelta}}</ref> All numbers are correlated with United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), if available.<ref group="Resource">{{Cite web |title=West and Central Africa |url=https://wca.humanitarianresponse.info/en |access-date=11 April 2015 |website=HumanitarianResponse.info |publisher=[[OCHA]]}}</ref> The reports are sourced from official information from the affected countries' health ministries. The WHO has stated the reported numbers "vastly underestimate the magnitude of the outbreak", estimating there may be 3 times as many cases as officially reported.<ref name="Reuters">{{Cite news |last=Miles, Tom |date=22 October 2014 |title=Official WHO Ebola toll near 5,000 with true number nearer 15,000 |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-health-ebola-who-idUSKCN0IB23220141022 |access-date=11 April 2015 |work=[[Reuters]]}}</ref><ref name="WHO 2014-08-22">{{Cite web |title=Ebola virus disease, West Africa – update 22 August 2014 |url=http://www.afro.who.int/en/clusters-a-programmes/dpc/epidemic-a-pandemic-alert-and-response/outbreak-news/4260-ebola-virus-disease-west-africa-22-august-2014.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140920193115/http://www.afro.who.int/en/clusters-a-programmes/dpc/epidemic-a-pandemic-alert-and-response/outbreak-news/4260-ebola-virus-disease-west-africa-22-august-2014.html |archive-date=20 September 2014 |access-date=18 September 2014 |publisher=WHO}}</ref>

===Understanding the data and its limitations===
Each row of the table represents the best available information cross-checked from multiple sources on the day it was reported. The data may be inaccurate for the following reasons:{{cn|date=February 2023}}
* Each data source or report may or may not include suspected cases that have not yet been confirmed.
* Each source or report may or may not include probable cases.
* Case numbers may be revised downward if a probable or suspected case is later found to be negative. <small>(Numbers may differ from reports as per respective Government reports. See notes at the bottom for stated source file.)</small>
* The reports usually refer to cumulative data totals since the start of the 2014 epidemic. When new data becomes available or old data is revised the correction could apply either to the past or the present.
* The number of deaths may be revised downwards if it is later found from testing those deaths were not from Ebola.
* There are variable delays in gathering, correcting and reporting the data from multiple sources.
* It is not possible to infer the rate of growth or decline in the spread of the disease from the cumulative data or the graphs; they simply reflect a timeline of the available data as reported on any given date. The real-world spread could be slowing while reported cumulative cases rise at a faster rate due to improved reporting, or the real-world spread could be increasing with flat cumulative data due to lack of reporting.
